title: The Merino Top Thrown Across a Lunch Table That Became Icebreaker
dek: In 1994 a sheep farmer handed Jeremy Moon a merino top; he mortgaged his house, bought into the farmer's company and spent half his first capital on the brand before making a garment.

story.event: Buying into a merino farmer's cottage business and building a brand before the first garment
story.summary: In 1994 the merino farmer Brian Brakenridge showed Jeremy Moon, a 24-year-old market researcher, a thermal top made from his own fibre. Moon quit his job, mortgaged his house, bought half of the Brakenridges' small business and raised about NZ$200,000 to NZ$250,000 from family and his network, then spent nearly half of it on brand development in early 1995 before any garment was made. The crude first range was sold to New Zealand outdoor shops; VF Corporation bought Icebreaker in 2018.
paragraphs: Some time in 1994, over lunch, a merino farmer named Brian Brakenridge threw a lightweight top across the table to Jeremy Moon, a 24-year-old marketing graduate working in market research. Moon pulled it on in the restaurant. "I'd grown up with wool as being itchy, prickly and heavy," he told Unlimited magazine in 2005. "This was light, soft, machine washable and gorgeous."

Brakenridge and his wife Fiona farmed merino on Pohuenui Island in the Marlborough Sounds and had a cottage business making thermal underwear from the fibre, sold mainly to tourists. Their wool fetched so little that most of it was bought for blending. "It was worse than a commodity, it was an additive," Brakenridge said. The outdoor clothing Moon knew was synthetic, cheap and proven, and wool had a bad name. He had recently been on a rainy sea-kayaking trip in synthetics, after which, he said, they "all stunk terribly after a few days".

He quit his job, mortgaged his house, bought half of the Brakenridges' company and spent three months on a business plan. A retired banker, Peter Travers, taught him to do financial projections and urged him to choose patient, influential investors. Investors from his network, among them friends' fathers and his own parents, put in about NZ$250,000 by Unlimited's account; later reports say NZ$200,000. Nearly half then went on the brand before a single garment was made. For six weeks in early 1995 Moon and a design team worked out what it stood for, with only a small piece of white merino fabric in front of them. Ice Breakers became Icebreaker, and the word wool gave way to merino. The chairman, Noel Todd, later admitted he often wondered whether it would work.

The first product was, in Moon's words, a "kind of confused thermal underwear", in blue or white. He and his first employee, Michelle Mitchell, each took one of New Zealand's islands with a suitcase of samples. Unlimited reported that 20 of the 60 retailers he targeted signed in the first year; a 2016 account says fourteen stores placed orders. There were mistakes, among them a run with sleeves six inches too short. In 2018 VF Corporation completed its purchase of the company, for a reported NZ$288 million.

quote.text: You know also that the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed and the desired impression is more readily taken.
quote.source_title: The Republic, tr. Benjamin Jowett, Project Gutenberg eBook #1497
quote.connection: Socrates is speaking of the stories told to children, which shape them before they can choose. Moon spent half his money on Icebreaker's story before it had a product, wagering that what the company stood for, settled early, would carry a crude first garment.

reflection: Some beginnings do not look like work. Six weeks of talking around a scrap of fabric would have looked, to an outsider, like people avoiding the real task, and the chairman wondered the same. Yet what they settled then shaped the choices that followed, down to the name of the fibre.

You are early in something too. If you have spent part of this week deciding what your work is for, rather than producing more of it, that may be the beginning Plato meant. Whatever you make first will probably be rough, as Moon's was, with its sleeves too short. That is allowed.
invitation: Write one sentence about what the work you are building is for, in words a stranger would understand. Make nothing else from it today.

cross_checks.claim: In 1994 a merino farmer showed the 24-year-old Moon a merino garment, which prompted the business
Moon quit his job and mortgaged his house to start Icebreaker
Start-up capital of roughly NZ$200,000 to NZ$250,000 came from family and friends' parents
VF Corporation completed its purchase of Icebreaker in 2018

research_notes: Start-up capital disagrees: Unlimited (2005), the most detailed and earliest account, says investors including Moon's parents put in a total of $250,000; the NZ Herald (2018) and Outside (2016) say $200,000; a sponsored NZ Herald piece (2021, cited only as a third support for the house loan) and a Stuff headline (2018, body not readable without JavaScript, not cited) mention $25,000 of Moon's own money. The story gives both investor figures with attribution and mentions the mortgage without an amount. Early retail uptake: Unlimited says 20 of 60 targeted retailers signed in the first year and the rest within two years; Outside says fourteen stores eventually booked orders from his first sales drive; the story gives both. The farmer's surname is spelt Brakenridge by Unlimited and Brackenridge by Outside; the story follows Unlimited, which interviewed him. Outside places the farmer in the Southern Alps, Unlimited on Pohuenui Island in the Marlborough Sounds; the story follows Unlimited. Moon's car on the first sales trips is a Datsun in Outside and a Ford Fairlane 500 in a later NZ Herald piece; the story mentions neither. The slate gave funding as bootstrapped, but the founder's mortgage was combined with outside investment from family and friends' parents, so funding is 'mixed'. Outside's piece ends with brand boilerplate and may have been produced with the company's involvement, so it is used only for Moon's own recollections and is not the sole support for any pivotal claim. VF did not disclose the price; NZ$288 million is the NZ Herald's figure. Outside reports a 1997 quality failure (shrinking, fraying shirts traced to a bad batch of wool) that led to long-term grower contracts; it is left out to keep the story to the founding episode. The Plato passage is about the stories told to young children in the education of the guardians; it is applied by analogy to a young company's story.
